title: Preserving the Cloud Castle's Heritage
task: Your class has attended a panel discussion on how governments can best protect ancient castles, libraries and forests. Notes: funding · tourism · education. Write an essay discussing TWO of the methods in your notes. Explain which method you think is more important, giving reasons. Write 220–260 words.

points.label: Discuss one method (funding, tourism or education)
Say which is more important and why

model:
Few would dispute that ancient castles, libraries and forests are worth protecting. The real question is how governments can do so most effectively, and two approaches stand out: direct funding and education.

The case for funding is obvious. Crumbling towers do not repair themselves, and without regular investment even the most famous sites can deteriorate beyond rescue within a generation. Government grants, perhaps financed through a modest tax on tourism, allow experts to carry out specialist restoration work that no volunteer group could afford. Admittedly, money alone is no guarantee of success, since poorly planned projects have sometimes damaged the very buildings they were meant to save.

Education, by contrast, works more slowly but reaches further. When schools take pupils to ancient forests and teach them the stories behind each stone, they create a generation that genuinely values its heritage. Such awareness has practical consequences: citizens who care about the past are more likely to vote for conservation, to report vandalism and to support local museums.

On balance, I would argue that education is the more important of the two. This is not to say that funding is unnecessary; in an emergency, only money can prevent a collapse. However, funding depends entirely on political will, and political will ultimately depends on what ordinary people care about. Only by teaching the young to treasure their heritage can we ensure that the money will still be there in fifty years' time.

title: Bringing Young Readers Back
task: Your class has listened to a radio discussion about how to encourage young people to read more. Notes: libraries · technology · families. Write an essay discussing TWO of the methods in your notes. Explain which method you think is more effective, giving reasons. Write 220–260 words.

points.label: Discuss one method (libraries, technology or families)
Say which is more effective and why

model:
It is often claimed that young people have abandoned books in favour of screens. Whether or not this is entirely true, there is general agreement that more could be done to nurture a love of reading, and both technology and families have a role to play.

Technology is frequently blamed for the problem, yet it may also offer part of the solution. Reading apps can recommend titles based on a child's interests, while e-books allow reluctant readers to adjust the font or listen along with an audio version. What is particularly striking is that many teenagers who claim to hate reading happily spend hours on online fan fiction, which suggests that the appetite for stories has not disappeared at all.

Families, conversely, shape reading habits long before any device does. A child who grows up surrounded by books, who sees their parents reading for pleasure and who is read to at bedtime is far more likely to become a lifelong reader. Admittedly, not every family has the time or the confidence to do this, particularly when parents work long hours.

All things considered, I believe that families are the more effective influence. Technology can certainly make reading more accessible, but it cannot create the emotional connection that turns reading into a habit. Consequently, rather than investing only in new apps, governments would be wise to support parents, for instance by giving free books to every newborn child and running reading workshops in local communities.

title: Proposal: A Festival for Cloud Castle
task: The Cloud Castle council wants to organise a new annual festival and has asked residents for proposals. Write a proposal describing the festival you would organise, explaining how it would benefit residents and suggesting how it could be funded and run. Write 220–260 words.
model:
Introduction
The aim of this proposal is to outline a new annual event, the Festival of Floating Lights, and to explain how it could be funded and organised at minimal cost to the council.

The festival
The festival would take place over one weekend each spring. During the day, the main square would host craft workshops, a storytelling competition for children and stalls selling local food. As night fell, residents would release hundreds of paper lanterns from the castle walls, followed by an open-air concert performed by local musicians.

Benefits for residents
Not only would the festival bring the community together, but it would also boost local businesses. Cafes and guesthouses would almost certainly benefit from the extra visitors, and young people would gain valuable experience by helping to run the event. Perhaps most importantly, it would give Cloud Castle a distinctive identity that residents could take pride in.

Funding and organisation
It is worth bearing in mind that the council's budget is limited. I would therefore suggest a combination of local business sponsorship and a small entrance fee for the evening concert. A committee of volunteers, supported by one council officer, could handle the planning, while the castle grounds would provide a free and spectacular venue.

Recommendation
I would strongly recommend that the council approves a trial festival next spring. If it proves successful, it could become a much-loved tradition for years to come.

title: Report: The Royal Library's Opening Hours
task: The head librarian of the Royal Library is considering three changes: opening later in the evening, opening at weekends, or starting an online lending service. Write a report evaluating at least two of these options and recommending the best one. Write 220–260 words.

points.label: Evaluate one option (evenings, weekends or online)

model:
Purpose
This report sets out to evaluate two of the proposed changes to the Royal Library's opening hours, namely weekend opening and an online lending service, and to recommend the more suitable option.

Weekend opening
The main advantage of opening on Saturdays and Sundays is that it would allow working adults and families to visit together. In a recent survey of readers, nearly half said that they rarely visit because the library is closed when they are free. A potential drawback, however, is cost: staff would have to be paid overtime, and heating the building for two extra days would add considerably to the energy bill.

Online lending
An online service, by contrast, would make thousands of e-books available at any hour, which would be particularly valuable for elderly readers and those living in remote villages. Although the initial investment in software would be significant, running costs would be relatively low. It should be noted, nevertheless, that some readers value the library as a meeting place, and an online service would do nothing to meet that need.

Recommendation
In light of the above, it is recommended that the library introduces online lending first, since it would reach the largest number of readers at the lowest long-term cost. Weekend opening could then be trialled on Saturday mornings only, which would allow the library to assess demand before committing to a more expensive timetable.

title: Review: A Book That Changed My Mind
task: A literary magazine is running a series called “A book that changed the way I think”. Write a review of a book (real or imaginary) briefly describing it, explaining how it changed your thinking and saying who would appreciate it. Write 220–260 words.
model:
The Cartographer of Clouds

At first glance, The Cartographer of Clouds looks like a simple children's adventure. The novel follows Ada, a young mapmaker who is ordered by the king to chart the kingdom's ever-changing sky. Yet behind this playful premise lies a surprisingly profound meditation on the limits of knowledge.

What sets the book apart is the way the author turns Ada's failure into its central theme. Every map she draws is out of date by the time the ink dries, and the king grows increasingly furious. Rather than rescuing her with a clever trick, the story allows Ada to accept that some things can only be understood, never controlled.

This made me reconsider my own obsession with planning. Like many students, I had always believed that with enough effort every outcome could be predicted. Ada's quiet acceptance gave me a new perspective: uncertainty is not a problem to be solved but a condition to be lived with, and there is a kind of freedom in that realisation.

Admittedly, the novel is not flawless. The middle chapters are slow at times, and some of the minor characters are rather thinly drawn. Nevertheless, the final pages are so moving that these weaknesses are easily forgiven.

I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who feels overwhelmed by pressure to have everything under control. Younger readers will enjoy the adventure, while older ones will find themselves thinking about it long after the last page.

title: Letter to the Editor: Save the Sky Bridge
task: Your local newspaper has published an article suggesting that the old Sky Bridge should be closed to save money. Write a letter to the editor explaining why the bridge matters to the community, responding to the argument about cost and suggesting an alternative. Write 220–260 words.
model:
Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to your article of 12 March, which suggested that the Sky Bridge should be closed in order to reduce the council's spending. While I appreciate that the council faces difficult choices, I believe this proposal would be a serious mistake.

For many residents, the bridge is far more than a convenient shortcut. It connects the eastern villages to the only hospital and secondary school in the area, and without it some families would face a journey of over an hour. Moreover, the bridge is part of our heritage: it has stood for three centuries and appears in countless local stories and paintings.

Your article argued that closing the bridge would save money on maintenance. However, this argument ignores the long-term costs. Extra bus services would have to be provided, local shops would lose customers and, once the structure is abandoned, repairing it later would be far more expensive than maintaining it now. In other words, the savings are short-term and largely illusory.

A far more sensible approach would be to share the cost. The council could introduce a small voluntary toll for tourists, who cross the bridge in large numbers during the summer, and invite local businesses to sponsor its upkeep. Rather than closing a vital link, the council should be looking for ways to protect it.

Yours faithfully,
Thomas Hale

title: Getting Young People Outdoors
task: Your class has watched a documentary about why many children now spend less time outdoors. Notes: school trips · technology · local parks. Write an essay discussing TWO of the ideas in your notes for getting young people outside more. Explain which idea you think is more effective, giving reasons. Write 220–260 words.

points.label: Discuss one idea (school trips, technology or local parks)
Say which is more effective and why

model:
It is widely accepted that children today spend far less time outdoors than their grandparents did. Of the many ideas proposed to reverse this trend, two seem particularly promising: school trips and better local parks.

School trips have the obvious advantage of reaching every pupil, regardless of their family's circumstances. A week spent camping, canoeing or tracking animals in a forest can transform a child's attitude to nature, and many adults still remember such experiences decades later. Admittedly, trips are expensive and happen only once or twice a year, so their effect may well fade once pupils return to their usual routines.

Improving local parks, by contrast, addresses the problem every single day. What many young people lack is not interest in the outdoors but somewhere safe and exciting to go after school. Were the council to invest in adventure playgrounds, cycle paths and wildlife ponds, children would be far more likely to spend their free time outside. Furthermore, parks bring families and neighbours together, which strengthens the whole community.

On balance, I would argue that local parks are the more effective solution. This is not to say that school trips are unimportant; they can spark a lifelong passion. However, a passion needs to be practised. Only by having green spaces close to home can children turn one exciting week into a lasting habit. Consequently, councils and schools should work together to ensure that every neighbourhood has a park worth visiting.

Introduction
The aim of this proposal is to suggest a new after-school Inventors' Club and to explain how it could be run within the school's limited budget.

What the club would offer
The club would meet every Thursday for an hour. Each term, members would work in small teams on a single project, such as a solar-powered car, a bird feeder that counts its visitors or a robot that waters the school plants. At the end of each term, the inventions would be displayed at a mini science fair to which parents are invited.

Benefits for students
Not only would the club make science more enjoyable, but it would also develop skills that are rarely practised in ordinary lessons. Designing, testing and improving a machine requires patience, teamwork and creative problem-solving. Perhaps most importantly, students who struggle with written work often shine when they can build something with their hands, so the club could boost the confidence of a wide range of pupils.

Organisation and equipment
Given that the budget is small, I would suggest using recycled materials wherever possible, alongside a few basic toolkits and two second-hand laptops for programming. In addition, the science teachers have already offered to take turns supervising, and older students could act as mentors to younger members.

Recommendation
I would therefore recommend that the club is launched as a trial next term. If it proves popular, it could become a permanent part of school life.

title: Report: Making Sports Day Better
task: Your PE teacher wants to make next year's Sports Day more enjoyable for everyone and has asked you for a report. Describe what went well this year, explain which parts were less successful and recommend changes. Write 220–260 words.
model:
Purpose
This report sets out to evaluate this year's Sports Day, based on a survey of 120 students, and to recommend changes for next year.

What went well
Overall, the event was a great success. The relay races were by far the most popular activity, with many students describing the atmosphere as electric. The decision to mix year groups in the teams was also widely praised, since it gave younger pupils the chance to make friends with older ones.

Less successful aspects
However, several problems were mentioned repeatedly. A recurring complaint was that students who are not particularly sporty spent most of the afternoon sitting on the grass with nothing to do. In addition, the timetable ran almost an hour late, which meant that the final races took place in the hottest part of the day. Arguably, the lack of shade and drinking water was the most serious issue, as a number of spectators felt unwell.

Recommendations
In light of the above, it is recommended that the programme includes a wider range of activities, such as an obstacle course, a three-legged race and a team quiz, so that every student can take part. Shorter heats would help to keep the timetable on track, and the event should start earlier in the morning to avoid the midday heat. Finally, a shaded rest area with free water should be provided throughout the day.

Were the school to adopt these changes, Sports Day would undoubtedly become an event that everyone looks forward to.

title: Review: Secrets of the Coral Kingdom
task: Your school magazine is starting a new “What to watch” page. Write a review of a nature documentary or series (real or imaginary), describing what it shows, evaluating how well it is made and saying who would enjoy it most. Write 220–260 words.
model:
Secrets of the Coral Kingdom

Rarely does a nature series manage to be both breathtaking and genuinely educational, but Secrets of the Coral Kingdom achieves exactly that. Over six episodes, it follows the creatures of a single reef in the Pacific Ocean, from tiny cleaner shrimps to a family of green turtles returning to the beach where they hatched.

What makes the series stand out is its extraordinary camera work. Using underwater drones, the film crew captured behaviour that had never been filmed before, including an octopus that collects shells to build itself a portable shelter. The footage is accompanied by a gentle, perfectly judged soundtrack, while the narrator explains complex ideas, such as how coral feeds, without ever talking down to the audience.

Admittedly, the series is not flawless. The fourth episode, which focuses on coral bleaching, is rather slow at times, and some viewers may find the scenes of damaged reefs upsetting. Nevertheless, these moments are important, because they show why the reef needs protecting, and the final episode ends on a hopeful note with a group of young divers replanting coral.

I would wholeheartedly recommend the series to anyone who is curious about the natural world. Younger viewers will be enchanted by the colourful fish and surprising animal tricks, whereas older students will appreciate the thoughtful message about caring for our oceans. It is, without doubt, the most memorable documentary I have watched this year.

task: Your class has been discussing how schools could become more environmentally friendly. Notes: recycling · transport · energy. Write an essay discussing TWO of the ideas in your notes. Explain which idea you think would make the bigger difference, giving reasons. Write 220–260 words.

model:
There is growing concern that schools, which use enormous amounts of paper, plastic and power, are not doing enough to protect the environment. Of the many changes that could be made, recycling and saving energy are perhaps the most widely discussed.

Improving recycling has the advantage of involving every pupil directly. Were the school to place clearly labelled bins in every classroom, students would soon develop habits that they might carry into adulthood. Admittedly, recycling alone does little to reduce the amount of waste produced in the first place, and many schools already have some form of scheme. Its impact, therefore, may well be limited.

Saving energy, by contrast, tackles one of the largest sources of a school's carbon emissions. Installing solar panels on the roof, replacing old light bulbs and switching off computers at the end of the day can cut electricity use dramatically. Furthermore, the money saved could be spent on books, trips or sports equipment, which would benefit everyone. The main drawback is the initial cost of the panels, although grants are often available to help with this.

On balance, I would argue that saving energy would make the bigger difference. What matters most is not how many bottles we sort, but how much energy we waste every single day. This is not to say that recycling is unimportant; rather, it should be part of a wider plan. Ultimately, a school that runs on sunshine sends a powerful message to every pupil who walks through its doors.

At present, young people in our town have remarkably few places to meet. The nearest park is a thirty-minute walk away, and the youth club closed last year. Consequently, many teenagers end up hanging around outside shops, which neither they nor the shopkeepers particularly enjoy. What we lack is not energy or enthusiasm, but a safe place in which to use them.

While I appreciate that parking near the high street is limited, I am not convinced that another car park is the answer. Arguably, it would simply encourage more traffic on roads that are already congested at school times.

Instead, I would like to propose that the land be used for a skate park with a small garden and seating area. Not only would this give young people somewhere active to spend their free time, but it would also provide a pleasant space for families and older residents. Introduction
The purpose of this report is to evaluate the Year 8 trip to the City Science Museum, based on a class survey, and to recommend whether it should be repeated.

Most valuable activities
By far the most memorable part of the day was the interactive space gallery, where students were able to steer a model rover across a Martian landscape. Almost every pupil rated it as excellent, and several said that it had made them consider becoming engineers. The live chemistry show, during which a presenter created a cloud of coloured smoke, was also extremely popular.

Areas for improvement
However, the visit was not without its problems. The museum was crowded with other school groups, so queues for the most popular exhibits sometimes lasted twenty minutes. It could be argued that the lunch break, which took place in a cold and noisy basement, was also rather too long. Furthermore, a number of students felt that their worksheets were so detailed that they spent more time writing than exploring.

Recommendations
In light of the above, it is recommended that the trip be repeated next year, as its educational value is clear. Were the school to book a weekday morning outside the busiest season, the queues would be far shorter. Replacing the worksheets with a short photo challenge would also allow students to engage more fully with the exhibits. With these changes, the trip could become a highlight of the school year.

title: Review: The Floating City
task: An international website for young film fans is asking for reviews of family films. Write a review of a film you have seen recently (real or imaginary), describing the story without giving away the ending, evaluating the acting and visual effects and saying who would enjoy it most. Write 220–260 words.
model:
The Floating City

Set in a world where entire towns drift above the clouds, The Floating City follows Kai, a shy boy who discovers that his home is slowly sinking towards the sea below. Together with his inventive best friend, Noor, he sets off on a daring journey to find the ancient engine that once kept the city in the air.

Where the film truly shines is in its visual effects. The sky islands, with their waterfalls tumbling into empty space, are nothing short of breathtaking, and the flying scenes are so convincing that the audience in my cinema actually gasped. Moreover, the young cast deliver impressive performances. Noor, in particular, is a brilliant character: clever, stubborn and genuinely funny, she steals almost every scene she appears in.

Admittedly, the film is not without its flaws. The villain, a greedy sky pirate, is rather predictable, and a subplot involving a lost royal crown seems to have been added simply to make the story longer. At times, the dialogue is also a little clumsy. Nevertheless, these weaknesses are easy to forgive, since the final half hour is as gripping as anything I have seen this year.

I would wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who enjoys adventure and fantasy, especially children aged eight and above. Younger viewers will be enchanted by the colourful creatures, while older ones will appreciate its thoughtful message about courage and friendship. Rarely have I left a cinema feeling quite so uplifted.

Introduction
The aim of this proposal is to suggest a fortnightly podcast, written and presented by students, which would help to keep the whole school community informed and connected.

Content
Each episode would last around fifteen minutes and include three regular features: a round-up of school news, an interview with a member of staff and a student spotlight celebrating achievements outside the classroom, from chess tournaments to charity bake sales. Listeners could also send in questions to be answered by the head teacher in a monthly special.

Benefits
Not only would the podcast give students a voice in school life, but it would also allow teachers to share information in a far more engaging way than a printed newsletter. Moreover, the team would develop valuable skills, such as interviewing, script writing and audio editing, which are rarely taught in ordinary lessons. Perhaps most importantly, quieter students who might never speak in assembly often find the confidence to express themselves through audio.

Requirements
Fortunately, the equipment needed is relatively inexpensive. Two good microphones, a pair of headphones and free editing software would be sufficient to begin with, and the music room could be used for recording at lunchtimes. The English department has kindly offered to supervise, and each episode would be shared on the school website.

Recommendation
I would therefore recommend that the podcast be launched as a trial next term. If it proves popular, it could become a permanent and much-loved part of school life.
